Manenberg - Batting for change

By: Floris Kotze | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A gangster turned coach - changing lives of many. One over at a time.

Unique Selling Point:
Research call with Shahied Adonis | Dlala Africa 
Shahied Adonis
Battingpro@gmail.com
064 411 5988
BACKGROUND:
Shahied Adonis grew up in the Cape Flats. When he was four years old, his father passed
away which eventually led him to a life of drugs that he later kicked.
He’s a professional cricket coach.
He worked for Old Mutual and was helping with their Sports program until Old Mutual
wanted to stop the program which was helping a lot of kids. Adonis got into a
disagreement with Old Mutual around this which eventually went to the Appeals court.
He won at the Appeals court and was dismissed by Old Mutual.
He was then employed by Cricket SA.
How this started – in 2012, his son wanted to get a bursary to get into Bishops but his
son played soccer. Adonis told him that he would need cricket or rugby to help him get
noticed by Bishops so for three years – he started training him, focusing on cricket and
in 2015 his son got the Bursary.
During this time, he realised that he could apply this to other children and try help them
as well. He built relationships with different schools and the community. He offered the
coaching clinics for free.
Coming from the Cape Flats, he had always wanted to find ways of giving back and this
was his opportunity.
This program was the cricket excellence program and he had a lot of kids from middle-
income family who came from a disadvantaged background.
In 2019, they moved to Primrose Park and he decided to take the program into a more
disadvantaged community. He didn’t really know much about Manenberg at the time –
just that it was a gang ridden, drug driven community. He decided to introduce himself
to the children there and immediately realised that that this was going to be a very
different challenge.
The children weren’t interested at all and he quickly realised that their issues were
different. The children were rude, they did drugs and lived with gangsters. On top of
that, these children were hungry.
In the first year, they didn’t even play any cricket – they got some soccer balls and
offered them a meal. He got some help from the community and some volunteers. With
time, the children started coming. Initially they had a very relaxed atmosphere, allowing
the children to do what they want in this now safe environment. They could chill and
listen to music…

In Manenberg – they used to use the school field but they often found bullet casings on
the field so they very quickly realised that they needed to move the program elsewhere.
In 2020, they started with the learning aids – food, cricket and soccer – and they could
come as and when they wanted.
They are up against the gangs in this area because the gangs want them as runners and
the gangs pay them like R100 a day and these kids use this money to take care of the
families they do have – mainly grandparents.
The Children struggle with reading right up to Grade 7. Most don’t have fathers and
some mothers themselves are drug addicts.
In Manenberg, there were no cricket nets so they got together with the community and
they built cricket pitches and had nets donated by Bishops (I think that’s the school he
mentioned).
With time, when they realised that the children would stay – that they would have a
structure.
So in 2020, they started paying the senior youths a stipend – they stepped up and
became part of the program and these kids who used to ‘bully’ them, became their role
models.
The key was that to be allowed in the program they now had participate in academic
lessons and play cricket. The key was providing them with food first and eventually
these kids started to buy into the program.
They’ve helped some children learn cricket and get Bursaries at Bishops, SACs and
Rondebosch as well.
One of their seniors got into club cricket as well.

Summary:
We follow Shahied Adonis and discover how a single person, can change the lives of many.

Script:



Montage of Manenberg, chaos…
Mumbled AUDIO
Link
Countless lives have been lost here, in the streets of Manenberg from gang-related crime drive-by shootings and drugs. Our story takes place here and the Cape flats but this time it's a little different, this time you'll be bowled over.
Pippa:
I've got it tip you off about the incredible work that is being done by a cricket coach in Primrose Park who is using the sports as a leg-up for youngsters that is so much more than encourage them to enjoy the game.
VO:
We got word about someone unique who was making a big difference in the poorest areas of the Cape Flats. So, we decided to pay him a visit…
VO:
We met him at the Cape Talk studios, as he was wrapping up a chat with talk show host, Pippa Hudson…
Claire: Guys, fantastic interview that I just heard.
Pippa: Thanks so much for picking up on this story.
VO: Shahied Adonis’s interview with Pippa caused quite a stir.
Pippa: In this case it was a cricket team, we got absolutely walloped by Shahied’s kids the other day.
VO: Shahied is a cricket coach, born and raised on the Cape Flats, a world away from the modern Cape Town studio. According to reports, 161 gang related murders were committed between April and June of last year. All of these murders occurred here, in areas like Manenberg on the Cape Flats.
He knows well the daily struggle of the area’s children.
Claire: Describe Shahied as a young boy.
Shahied: Probably the period when the naughtiness took over and getting involved in drugs in my case I never had a father, he passed away when I was 4. The idle time I would say, is the biggest enabler that kinda gets you to do things after school and it kinda takes you down the wrong path.
I always say cricket saved my life. When it comes to drugs is relapse and relapse.
So you need something that kinda teaches you discipline, commitment and you gotta have the fun factor as well.
VO: And so, Shahied's love for cricket, and wanting to help his community, developed into something unique.
LINK: Shahied has one goal, to keep as many kids as possible out of the gangs. How is he doing it? Simple, with this.
Shahied: Cricket takes a lot of time. The fact that you have the passion for the game, obviously will keep you in it. And it started slowly, you had a few kids and the word just spread. I think our success was basically providing a hot meal.
VO: His vision of creating something bigger than just a cricket centre, started to take shape a few years ago when he launched Dlala Africa, a non profit organisation relying entirely on donations. Boys and girls from surrounding areas are encouraged to go to Manenberg cricket grounds after school. Not only to play sports, but to study together and get something to eat. It keeps them off the streets and out of harm's way.
Shahied: We try to provide everything, from Sanitary towels, the key is to provide the food.
Serena: Compared to a normal child’s life, they are missing obviously a meal, they are not getting three meals a day, they don’t have the equipment, the resources obviously.
VO: Serena Beukes is a psychology undergraduate who’s tutoring some of the kids in Shahied’s programme.
Serena: The outer layer is obviously going to be hard and aggressive because that is what they are going through in their daily lives. They need to protect themselves, they need to have their guard up, but once you get to know them, you converse with them, you spend time with them, it’s completely different they’re just children and they just need that love and affection that they’re not maybe getting at at home…

Serena: I actually spoke to a few girls, it is a difficult one actually. They experienced rape. How does someone do that to the next person? Being raped by someone she knows.

Claire: That’s the real world experience that these children are living in.

Serena: Yes, this is what they are facing and people would come to me and say but would you do, why do you turn to drugs? But, this is their lives, it’s a harsh reality that they are living in.
Shahied: We have kids currently that are in grade 5, 6, 7 that can’t read. We want to take that to the next level where we have quality, quality tutors to provide that professional tutoring system.
VO: Although the programme has been going for a few years, providing for the children is a struggle. Shahied’s daily routine consists of picking up donations from all over town and driving to Manenberg to feed the ever increasing number of hungry mouths.
Shahied: For kids that live in those areas, starvation is right on top of the list. Malnutrition in today’s time, which is a shock.
Claire: They are in survival mode, it sounds.
Shahied: Big time. That’s the only way, you are not going to find a kid just come walking down just to play sport, it is actually the food.
VO: During our time with Shahied in Manenberg, the threat of danger was ever-present… Just recently, a child was killed, when a rival gang opened fire on 7 kids who were standing outside a block of flats. It happened just down the street from Shahied’s cricket ground.
Shahied: All 7 kids that were shot was basically just innocent bystanders. Few weeks after that, they shot a 9 year old boy in the head and a 17 year old. The 9 year old died, I think 3, 4 days later. The 17 year old died on the scene. These people are fed up now with the Government, they are saying they can’t live in fear, not knowing if a kid is walking from here to the shop across the road, if they’ll come back.
Serena: It's not as easy as you think to change things to get out that whole poverty stricken environment, it's not easy to charge in the overnight either, but there is bursaries there is opportunities
VO: And this is the target that Shahied is chasing, to add more kids to the list of 11 who’ve already received bursaries at more affluent schools.
Shahied: Bursary after bursary those moments when I am sitting here and the deal is closed and I know this kid is going to Bishops, or Sax, that’s the moment you realise, you know, you just have to keep going and it is the energiser.
Shaun: We are Very keen to make sure that not only Bishops boys get to experience the fantastic facilities on this campus.
VO: Shaun Hewett heads up cricket at Diocesan College, or Bishops, a private school in the suburb of Rondebosch, where a few of Shahied’s boys have secured full bursaries.
Claire: What is entailed in that?
Shaun:
Full Tuition, from literally grade 8 to grade 12. Boarding house, it's all tours paid for, cricket kit, if they need new cricket boots, new cricket bat, new cricket bag, whatever it might be the school will certainly assist in that regard
Where Shahied is very good, once the boys are in the system you don't really hear from the mentors again, until they're in Matriculate,but Shahied is there with the guys all the way through. He remind the boys that they very lucky to be here.
VO: One of the boys is Bishop’s opening batsman, Adnaan Lagadien. He was the first Manenberg boy to receive a bursary.
Adnaan:
Everything changed after I went to train with him, he trained me to become a cricketer I am today. I hope to become 1st Province u19 and then make it to SA U19, and then take it from there.
Shahied: When we go to Bishop I remind them, do not chirp hey, because we want to be invited back, don’t go too hard. But enjoy… I always tell them, it’s the friendship game, remember, these are our friends. And we have played over a hundred matches at Bishops. And I can use it, if you guys don’t tow in line, if you don’t listen, you are not going to Bishops, you are not going to make the team.
Claire: Hi Coach you are harsh hey?
Shahied:
I am! Otherwise you lose the discipline, and you don’t want to lose discipline.
Shahied: If the don’t make it as a professional cricketer, their work ethic, their commitment to self development, that would kind of stand in good state to find a professional career.
And if we can get them through that age of getting shot or stabbed, I’d say that is great as well.
LINK: A lot of people have written-off Manenberg, they say the bad far outweighs the good, but with people like Shahied who still believe in the children in this community hopefully things can turn around.

When he was four years old, his father passed away which eventually led him to a life of drugs that he later kicked. He’s a professional cricket coach. He worked for Old Mutual and was helping with their Sports program until Old Mutual wanted to stop the program which was helping a lot of kids. Adonis got into a disagreement with Old Mutual around this which eventually went to the Appeals court. He won at the Appeals court and was dismissed by Old Mutual. He was then employed by Cricket SA. How this started – in 2012, his son wanted to get a bursary to get into Bishops but his son played soccer. Adonis told him that he would need cricket or rugby to help him get noticed by Bishops so for three years – he started training him, focusing on cricket and in 2015 his son got the Bursary. During this time, he realised that he could apply this to other children and try help them as well. He built relationships with different schools and the community. He offered the coaching clinics for free. Coming from the Cape Flats, he had always wanted to find ways of giving back and this was his opportunity. This program was the cricket excellence program and he had a lot of kids from middle- income family who came from a disadvantaged background. In 2019, they moved to Primrose Park and he decided to take the program into a more disadvantaged community. He didn’t really know much about Manenberg at the time – just that it was a gang ridden, drug driven community. He decided to introduce himself to the children there and immediately realised that that this was going to be a very different challenge. The children weren’t interested at all and he quickly realised that their issues were different. The children were rude, they did drugs and lived with gangsters. On top of that, these children were hungry. In the first year, they didn’t even play any cricket – they got some soccer balls and offered them a meal. He got some help from the community and some volunteers. With time, the children started coming. Initially they had a very relaxed atmosphere, allowing the children to do what they want in this now safe environment. They could chill and listen to music… In Manenberg – they used to use the school field but they often found bullet casings on the field so they very quickly realised that they needed to move the program elsewhere. In 2020, they started with the learning aids – food, cricket and soccer – and they could come as and when they wanted. They are up against the gangs in this area because the gangs want them as runners and the gangs pay them like R100 a day and these kids use this money to take care of the families they do have – mainly grandparents. The Children struggle with reading right up to Grade 7. Most don’t have fathers and some mothers themselves are drug addicts. In Manenberg, there were no cricket nets so they got together with the community and they built cricket pitches and had nets donated by Bishops (I think that’s the school he mentioned). With time, when they realised that the children would stay – that they would have a structure. So in 2020, they started paying the senior youths a stipend – they stepped up and became part of the program and these kids who used to ‘bully’ them, became their role models. The key was that to be allowed in the program they now had participate in academic lessons and play cricket. The key was providing them with food first and eventually these kids started to buy into the program. They’ve helped some children learn cricket and get Bursaries at Bishops, SACs and Rondebosch as well. One of their seniors got into club cricket as well.
metadata.Summary: We follow Shahied Adonis and discover how a single person, can change the lives of many.
